\[
n_2\mid 7\qquad\text{and}\qquad n_2\equiv 1\pmod 2.
\]
Hence $n_2=1$ or $n_2=7$.

Suppose that $n_2=7$. The conjugation action of $G$ on its seven Sylow $2$-subgroups gives a homomorphism $\varphi:G\to S_7$. Its kernel is normal in $G$. If $G$ were simple, then $\ker\varphi$ would be either trivial or all of $G$. The action is nontrivial, since a trivial action would make every Sylow $2$-subgroup normal, contradicting their being distinct. Thus $\ker\varphi$ is trivial, so $\varphi$ is injective.

Therefore $G$ would be isomorphic to a subgroup of $S_7$, forcing $|G|=224$ to divide $|S_7|=5040$ by Lagrange's theorem. This is impossible, since $224\nmid 5040$. Hence $n_2\ne 7$, so $n_2=1$. The unique Sylow $2$-subgroup has order $32$ and is normal. It is a proper nontrivial subgroup of $G$, so $G$ is not simple.
\end{proof}
